FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Discuss common hand and wrist injuries in the athletic patient population.
Review decision making with regard to surgical versus nonsurgical management of hand and
wrist injuries in the athletic patient population to achieve the best outcomes.
Discuss rehabilitation of hand and wrist injuries and specific outcomes in athletes.
Initial Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History and Mechanism of Injury
Exact mechanism of injury (ie, collision, fall, direct impact)
Subluxation or dislocation, even if self-reduced, especially the direction of initial displacement,
should be noted.

Handedness and level of sports participation
Physical Examination
Visual assessment
Assess for laceration, swelling, ecchymosis, or gross deformity, including rotational deformity
of the digits.
Palpation
Palpate areas of concern for tenderness.
Assesses competency of collateral ligamentous structures, evaluating the degree of laxity
and end point, with the joint in full extension and 30° of flexion.
Assess for masses: Stener lesion (retracted ulnar collateral ligament [UCL]) at the thumb
metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint
A retracted or bowstringing tendon may be palpated volarly.
Range of motion
Differentiate a contracture (active and passive motion are the same) from a lag (passive
motion is greater than active motion)
Flexor tendons—Evaluate each joint individually to isolate the flexor digitorum profundus
(FDP) tendon and the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon separately in each digit
Extensor tendons
At the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint level, assess for extension while stabilizing the digit
at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and MCP joints.
At the PIP joint level, perform the Elson test (excessive extension at the DIP joint with a
passively hyperflexed PIP joint suggests a central slip injury).
MCP joint level
Place the hand flat, and evaluate ability to elevate the digits off the table.
Tendon subluxation or lack of active MCP joint extension in combination with the ability
to hold the digit after passive extension suggests a sagittal band injury.
Perform a thorough neurovascular examination.
On-Field Management
If gross deformity is noted, gentle reduction and splinting should be performed.
An obviously dislocated joint should be expediently reduced.

If available, a digital block with local anesthetic will greatly facilitate fracture or dislocation
reduction and post-reduction motion evaluation.
If concern for digital nerve injury exists, a repeat examination can be performed after the
anesthetic has worn off.
After reduction, immediate return to play with buddy taping may be possible in patients with a
simple dislocation (particularly interphalangeal finger joints), full motion, and clinical stability.
Select athletes with a displaced but non–limb-threatening injury may return to play in a
protective splint or a mitten cast after a thorough discussion of the risks if the risks of
additional injury are minimized and treatment is sought promptly afterward.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard views of the injured extremity are obtained; for a finger injury, dedicated finger
radiographs are preferred.
Assess joint congruency and alignment.
CT
Indicated for complex intra-articular fractures or fracture-dislocations
Can assess difficult to image carpal injuries, such as hook of the hamate fractures
MRI
Indicated to assess soft-tissue injury or pathology
May allow for earlier diagnosis and expedited treatment or return to play decisions in
patients with some fractures, such as a scaphoid fracture
Finger Joint Dislocations
Overview
Ligamentous injuries about the DIP, PIP, and MCP joints (PIP joint most commonly) frequently
are observed during athletic competition.
Epidemiology
More than 160,000 finger dislocations were managed in U.S. emergency departments between
2004 and 2008.1
Often observed in athletes who play basketball and football
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Injuries of the Hand and Wrist
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004081
3/37

Injury to the PIP joint is the most common ligamentous injury to the hand. In the National
Football League (NFL), PIP joint dislocations comprised 17% of hand injuries.2
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The most common direction is dorsal dislocation from a hyperextension injury to the joint with
axial compression, resulting in volar plate and collateral injury, commonly from a ball striking
the digit and causing hyperextension deformity.
Volar dislocation from hyperflexion injury to the joint with axial compression; central slip may
be injured.
Lateral dislocation: injury to the collateral ligament and likely partial avulsion of the volar plate
MCP joint dislocations
Dorsal dislocation occurs more often than volar dislocation; volar plate often is interposed
and prevents reduction.
Dorsal dislocation
Occurs with hyperextension and high-energy axial load forces
Most common MCP joint dislocation involves the index finger
Fracture-dislocation
PIP joint fracture-dislocation: injuries with or without joint instability; usually involve the volar
lip of the middle phalanx.
Imaging Studies
On lateral radiographs, rule out persistent dorsal subluxation3 (Figure 1.)

Figure 1 Illustrations of a normal digit (top) and a subluxated digit (bottom) show the dorsal V
sign described by Light, which is observed on a lateral radiograph. The V sign indicates
proximal interphalangeal joint subluxation and that the articular surfaces are not congruent or
parallel. (Reproduced with permission from Blazar PE, Steinberg DR: Fractures of the proximal
interphalangeal joint. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2000;8[6]:383-390.)
Management
The goal is to allow for early range of motion through a stable arc while maintaining joint
congruence.
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
DIP joint dislocations
Perform closed reduction; after reduction, the DIP joint should be held in 0° to 20° of
flexion for at least 2 to 3 weeks.
After splinting is completed, continue to protect the joint via buddy taping of the digit.
Depending on position and sport, athletes may be able to safely return to play after closed
reduction and with the use of a finger splint or buddy taping.
PIP joint dislocations
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Injuries of the Hand and Wrist
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004081
5/37

Under a digital block, perform closed reduction and buddy taping for simple dorsal or
lateral dislocations to allow for active motion.
Axial traction in combination with slight exaggeration of the deformity and distally
directed pressure over the middle phalanx will allow the joint to reduce.
Immediately after the reduction, assess stability by asking the patient to perform a full arc
of active range of motion.
Lateral radiographs, especially in full extension, should demonstrate a fully concentric
joint; dynamic fluoroscopy may be helpful to assess stability during motion.
If the joint is stable through the full arc of motion, range of motion should be encouraged,
and the finger can be buddy taped to the adjacent digit for 3 to 6 weeks.
Immediate return to play may be allowed if buddy taping and/or the use of a glove
affords adequate protection.
Can use extension block splinting for 4 to 6 weeks for a dorsal dislocation that is unstable
after reduction
For volar PIP joint dislocations, apply an extension splint for 6 to 8 weeks to protect the
central slip.
Reduction maneuver should include flexion of the MCP joint to relax the lateral bands.
The central slip should be assessed via the Elson test; if compromised, the PIP joint
should be splinted in extension for 6 to 8 weeks while beginning immediate DIP joint
motion to avoid scarring of the lateral bands.
PIP joint fracture-dislocation
Volar lip fractures involving less than 30% of the articular surface usually are stable after
reduction and can be managed in a fashion similar to that for a simple dorsal dislocation.
Unstable PIP joint dislocations with persistent subluxation in full extension can be managed
nonsurgically via extension block splinting set at 10° to 20° less extension than the point at
which the joint is stable.
MCP joint dislocations
Reduction maneuver—An intra-articular block with a local anesthetic is performed.
Importantly, traction should be avoided. Reduction is performed by applying direct
pressure over the prominent base of the proximal phalanx, allowing it to slide into the joint.
Refrain from multiple reduction attempts at the MCP joint given concern for interposition
of the volar plate, lumbricals, or flexor tendons.
After reduction of the MCP joint dislocation, the digit should be splinted with the wrist in
slight extension and the MCP joint in 30° to 60° of flexion for 3 to 6 weeks, followed by
buddy taping for an additional 2 to 3 weeks

Outcomes4
Outcomes of simple dislocations managed via early motion generally are good and tend to
be better compared with brief immobilization.
Stiffness and contractures are common if mobilization is delayed, and aggressive hand
therapy may be necessary.
Early return to play may be possible, even if a dorsal blocking splint is used, given that
adequate protection, such as a mitten cast, is used.
Surgical Management
Indications
Irreducible dislocations
Displaced dorsal lip fractures of the middle phalanx in PIP joint fracture-dislocations with
incongruent articulation and/or joint surface
Volar lip fractures involving more than 50% of the articular surface are more likely to be
unstable and to require surgical management.
Techniques
Techniques used include trans-articular pinning; extension block pinning; external fixation;
volar plate arthroplasty; open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with the use of Kirschner
wires, mini screws, a plate, or cerclage wire; tension-band wiring; and hemihamate
arthroplasty.
Reduction of MCP joint dislocation (Video 1)
SEND FEEDBACK

7/37

Video 1 Tuckman DV: Open Reduction of an Irreducible MCP Dislocation [video]. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-
page/22846__Videos. Accessed July 28, 2021.
Rehabilitation
Athletes with a simple dislocation who are treated via buddy taping can return to play after
pain subsides. The largest risk of returning to play early is repeat dislocation of the joint and
worsening instability.
Early return to play after surgical fixation or in patients with a more complex injury is possible
if the digit can be adequately protected.
Outcomes
Postoperative arcs of motion after ORIF of PIP joint fracture-dislocations range from 70° to
100°.4-8
Missed or delayed diagnosis, especially of PIP joint fracture-dislocations, may lead to chronic
deformity, such as boutonnière or swan neck deformities.4-8
Metacarpal Fractures

Overview
Frequently observed injuries, especially in athletes involved in contact sports, such as football
or rugby, and athletes involved in sports in which high-velocity objects strike the hand, such as
baseball or hockey
Epidemiology
Metacarpal fractures are common injuries of the hand
Metacarpal fractures make up approximately 18% of fractures reported in the United States.9
The incidence of metacarpal fractures in the United States each year is more than 250,000,
most of which occur in young men.9
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most common mechanism of injury is a fall onto the hand or a direct blow to the hand at the
level of the metacarpal.
Often direct blow injuries result from an individual striking another individual or a hard object,
especially in athletics.
Injury Classification
Fracture pattern classification: transverse, short versus long oblique, spiral, comminuted; apex
dorsal angulation is most common in the shaft and neck (Boxer’s fracture).
Metacarpal head fractures are rare but may lead to dysfunction in the MCP joint.
Metacarpal base fractures
Often involve the ring and little fingers
Wrist extensor tendon attachment acts as a displacing force
Intra-articular thumb metacarpal base fractures
Bennett: partial intra-articular
Rolando: complete intra-articular
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications

Metacarpal head fractures: nondisplaced intra-articular fractures without evidence of
ligamentous injury
Acceptable angulations for shaft and neck fractures are listed in Table 1.10,11

With more angulation, alterations in the flexor tendon mechanism may be present and an
extension lag is possible.
A 7° extensor lag is associated with every 2 mm of shortening at the fracture site.9
Metacarpal base fractures: nondisplaced intra-articular fractures without evidence of
disruption of the carpometacarpal joints or evidence of avulsion injury from the extensor
tendons
Rotational deformity must be minimal because it is poorly tolerated.
Techniques/procedures
Jahss reduction technique: involves flexion of the MCP and PIP joints to 90° and applying a
dorsal force to the metacarpal head via the proximal phalanx12
After reduction, surgeons must reassess if persistent rotational deformity is present.
Thumb base fractures
Closed reduction maneuver includes applying traction with pronation and palmar
abduction of the thumb while placing counterpressure on the radial aspect of the
metacarpal base.13
Nonsurgical fracture management
The carpometacarpal and MCP joints need to be immobilized in an intrinsic plus position or a
thumb spica cast, depending on the injured metacarpal, after closed reduction.
The patient’s hand can be placed into a radial gutter, ulnar gutter, or outrigger splint to
provide adequate immobilization with motion of the other digits.
Outcomes

Athletes who are treated nonsurgically usually are those who compete at lower levels or
those injured during the off-season.
Normally, athletes can be treated nonsurgically via a short period of immobilization (3 to 4
weeks), depending on the fracture, and can return to play with the use of a protective splint
or mitten cast as the bone heals.
Full motion and excellent functional outcomes usually are achieved.9
Surgical Management
Indications
In general, surgical treatment is indicated in patients with multiple, unstable, or irreducible
fractures of the metacarpals, if angulation exceeds acceptable parameters, or if articular
surface displacement is greater than 1 mm.
Metacarpal neck fractures—Athletes are more likely to require anatomic reduction because
the prominence of the metacarpal head in the palm may lead to difficulty with
grasping/gripping.
Surgical treatment in athletes may permit faster return to play.
Surgical fracture fixation
Kirschner wires are a standard option for hand fracture fixation; however, more rigid fixation
should be considered in athletes to allow for earlier return to sports activity.
Lag screw fixation, headless screws, intramedullary devices, and plates allow for early
motion and potentially faster return to sport (Figure 2; Video 2).
Figure 2 Radiographs of hands demonstrate internal fixation of metacarpal fractures. A,
Oblique radiograph of a hand with a spiral fourth metacarpal shaft fracture. PA (B) and
oblique (C) radiographs demonstrate open reduction and internal fixation with the use of
lag screws. Oblique radiographs of a hand with a Rolando fracture before (D) and after (E)

open reduction and internal fixation.(Courtesy of Lauren Santiesteban, MD, New York, NY,
and Igor Immerman, MD, San Francisco, CA.)
Postoperative management
Splinting, if performed, is in intrinsic plus position. Early motion with removable splints is a
benefit of rigid fixation and is critical for early return to play.
Can remove the splint at 3 to 4 weeks postoperatively to allow for active MCP joint range of
motion.
Video 2 Hoang D, Cherones AL, Huang JI: Metacarpal Fractures: Antegrade Intramedullary Headless
Screw Fixation [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2020. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/21616__Videos. Accessed July 28, 2021.
Rehabilitation
Protective splints or well-padded mitten casts can be used for protection during practices or
competition events.
Early range of motion balanced with prevention of additional injury permits safe, early return
to sport.14,15
For example, football athletes with a Bennett fracture in their nonthrowing hand or who play
nontackling positions can return to contact play 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively with the use of

a protective splint,14 whereas those with involvement of the throwing hand or those involved
in tackling positions can return to play 6 to 10 weeks postoperatively with the use of a
protective splint.14
Outcomes
Internal fixation is associated with a high rate of healing.16,17
Return to play ranges from 1 day to more than 3 weeks with appropriate protective
splinting.16,17
Thumb Collateral Ligament Injuries
Overview
Collateral ligamentous injuries to the MCP joint of the thumb, including the radial and ulnar
collateral ligaments, are common in athletes.
These injuries may lead to a generalized pain or ache about the MCP joint, which may lead to
difficulty in gripping activities and difficulty with pinch strength.
Skier’s thumb is a frequently used term for an acute UCL injury of the MCP joint of the thumb.
Epidemiology
UCL injuries have been described as comprising 86% of the injuries to the thumb MCP joint.18
In general, these injuries occur at a rate ten times higher than radial collateral ligament (RCL)
injuries.18
RCL injuries are observed less frequently.18
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
UCL injuries frequently are referred to as a skier’s thumb; however, they can occur during any
sporting activity after a fall onto an outstretched hand in which a radially (valgus) directed
force with hyperabduction of the MCP joint occurs.
These injuries also occur if an object strikes the ulnar aspect of the thumb.
RCL injuries also frequently occur during athletic activities but require an ulnarly direct force
on the MCP joint of the thumb, which may occur during a fall onto the radial aspect of the
thumb or if an object strikes the radial aspect of the thumb.

Risk Factors
Repetitive activities that lead to radial or ulnar stress on the MCP joint
In addition, these injuries can occur with one-time radial or ulnar stress to the MCP joint that
leads to a partial or full tear of the ligament.
Injury Classification
Grading of tears of the UCL or RCL:18,19
Grade 1: incomplete; pain without appreciable instability on physical examination.
Grade 2: partial; pain with laxity on physical examination with a firm end point.
Grade 3: complete; pain with laxity on physical examination without a firm end point.
Physical Examination
Stress examination of the MCP joint via radial and ulnar deviation in 30° of flexion (proper
collateral ligament) and in full extension (accessory collateral ligament and/or volar plate)
In general, instability of more than 30° to 15° compared with the contralateral thumb
indicates a complete tear.18
Palmar subluxation stress examination: greater than 3 mm indicates a complete tear18
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Stress imaging examination of the MCP joint via radial and ulnar deviation to examine for
joint widening and instability may be helpful.
MRI or ultrasonography: can be used as an adjunct if collateral ligament injury is suspected20
Differential Diagnosis
Acute versus chronic tears
Tears are considered subacute more than 3 weeks after the initial injury.
Tears are considered chronic 3 to 4 months after initial injury.
Partial versus full ligamentous injuries
Associated volar plate involvement
Associated avulsion fractures

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Grade 1 or grade 2 ligamentous injuries
Nondisplaced bony avulsion injuries
Techniques/procedures
Immobilize the MCP joint and protect it from varus- or valgus-directed forces (depending on
the injured ligament) for 4 to 6 weeks.21
Athletes with a minor injury who participate in noncontact sporting activities can return to
play with the use of protective splinting 2 to 4 weeks postinjury.21
Athletes who participate in contact sports, athletes with more severe injuries, and athletes
who are prone to repeat injury may require longer immobilization (6 weeks) before
returning to play.21
Depending on the sport and the position, earlier return to play with the use of a protective
cast or splint may be possible. For example, a football lineman can have a mitten cast
applied on top of the thumb splint to afford additional protection.
Outcomes
Nonsurgical management of bony avulsion fractures leads to overall high satisfaction, return
of pinch and grip strength, and a high rate of return to work and sports activity despite a
relatively high (25% to 60%) rate of radiographic nonunion.19,22
Nonsurgical management of complete soft-tissue UCL injury has been reported to result in
good or satisfactory outcomes in 85% to 90% of patients; however, the presence of a Stener
lesion is associated with poorer outcomes.23-25
Surgical Management
Indications
Grade 3 ligamentous injuries
Presence of a Stener lesion
The adductor aponeurosis is interposed beneath the avulsed ligament, preventing
anatomic healing.21
Displaced avulsion fractures

Techniques/procedures—Many possible configurations for UCL or RCL ligamentous repair
exist, including but not limited to suture anchors, suture buttons, interference screws, bone
tunnels with sutures, and internal brace augmentation.26-28 Ligament reconstruction with
autograft or allograft is used for subacute or chronic injury or if repair is deemed impossible
intraoperatively. Dorsal capsule repair is an important aspect of repair (Video 3).
Video 3 Tuckman DV: Thumb Ulnar Collateral Ligament Repair With Internal Brace Augmentation
[video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2020. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/22879__Videos. Accessed July 28, 2021.
Postoperative management
Depending on the fixation technique, the thumb is immobilized in a thumb spica splint for 2
to 6 weeks, followed by protected range of motion exercises.
Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation
Commonly, a protective splint is used during contact sports for at least 3 months.18
Internal brace augmentation has been reported to shorten the rehabilitation period and allow
for earlier return to sports activity.28,29

Outcomes
Sochacki et al30 reviewed 23 NFL players who underwent surgical fixation of a UCL injury, with
return to sports activity defined as at least one NFL game postoperatively.
Of the 23 players, 22 were able to return to sports activity at mean of 132.2 days (± 126.1
days)
The 1-year NFL career survival rate was 87%.
Morse et al31 examined 137 forearm and hand injuries in the National Basketball Association.
Nine of these injuries included thumb ligament tears, all of which required surgical fixation.
The thumb ligamentous injuries were associated with the longest time to return to play
(mean, 67.5 days ± 17.7 days), which was statistically significant compared with other hand
injuries.
Tendinous Injuries of the Digits
Overview/Epidemiology
Mallet finger
Injury to the terminal extensor mechanism of the finger
May be purely tendinous or involve a dorsal lip fracture of the distal phalanx
Most common tendon injury observed in athletes
Jersey finger
Avulsion injury of FDP tendon
May be a purely tendinous or a bony avulsion; occasionally a combination of bony and
tendinous injury.
Dissimilar from most mallet finger injuries, FDP avulsions are almost uniformly managed
surgically.
Pulley injuries
Injury to the flexor sheath often is subtle and may be difficult to recognize.
If unmanaged, considerable motion limitations and finger contractures may be observed.
Tendinous injuries occur during various sports, particularly contact sports, such as basketball
and football. Mallet finger often results from a jammed finger, as seen in basketball, volleyball,
baseball, soccer, football, and rugby players. Most of the injuries occur in the ulnar three digits
in the dominant hand.32-38

9/3/26, 7:25 AM
AAOS | Athletic Injuries of the Hand and Wrist
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004081
17/37

Classically, FDP avulsion is observed in American football players (and athletes who participate
in similar sports, such as rugby) who grab an opponent’s jersey, resulting in the colloquial
name for this injury. These injuries are most common in the ring finger.34
Flexor pulley injuries classically are observed in rock climbers, accounting for 20% of climbing
injuries in one series.38 In a study of 42 elite competitive rock climbers, clinically evident
bowstringing was observed in 26%, and as many as 24% possibly had an isolated A2 pulley
rupture without bowstringing.39 Other athletes, including weightlifters, baseball players, and
football players, also may sustain this injury.40-42 During rock climbing, pulleys can be
subjected to a force as great as 700 N.43,44 Long and ring fingers are most at risk during
climbing.45 Bowstringing of the tendon results in a flexion contracture. The A2 and A4 pulleys
are the most important biomechanically and are at the greatest risk for injury.46
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Mallet finger
Forceful axial load against the fingertip resulting in sudden, forceful flexion of the DIP joint as
it is in active extension, resulting in extensor avulsion
Sharp laceration of the extensor tendon
Hyperextension injury is a less common etiology.36
Jersey finger
Sudden, forceful active finger flexion against resistance
Forceful load on the fingertip, resulting in hyperextension of the DIP joint and avulsion of the
flexor mechanism
Pulley injury
High-force active flexion or gripping, such as during rock climbing.
Crimping holds place extreme load on the flexor mechanism, and the loads approach
maximum failure points of the pulley mechanism.47 In addition, a slip or loss of a foot hold
may cause a sudden overload of the finger and, therefore, rapidly increase the load on the
pulley system. Climbers may report a pop with subsequent swelling in the digit and pain with
grip. 
Imaging Studies
Radiographs

Radiographs of the finger (AP and lateral views) are necessary to evaluate for bony avulsion
and joint subluxation.
MRI and ultrasonography
MRI is a sensitive imaging modality to diagnose tendon and pulley injuries in the hand.48,49
Ultrasonography allows for dynamic imaging, which is useful to visualize tendon gliding and
bowstringing.44
Mallet Finger Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Most mallet finger injuries may be managed nonsurgically with good results.
Techniques/procedures
Extension splinting
Outcomes
Outcomes of splinting generally are excellent, with high patient satisfaction and no
considerable functional deficits.33,50-52
Indications include closed soft-tissue tendon avulsions and closed fractures that involve less
than 30% of the joint articular surface without joint subluxation. Evidence shows that, even in
patients with considerable joint involvement and DIP joint subluxation, closed management
results in good outcomes with joint remodeling.50,51
The DIP joint should be immobilized in full extension or a few degrees of hyperextension.
The splint may be applied volarly or dorsally and can be off-the-shelf or custom-made. No
considerably clinically important difference has been demonstrated between the various
splinting options. The PIP joint should remain free and motion should be encouraged to
avoid stiffness. The splint is worn full time for 8 weeks, followed by range of motion exercises
and 4 additional weeks of part-time wear.
Surgical Management
Indications
Open injuries
Pediatric physeal injuries (Seymour fracture)
Bony mallet injuries with joint subluxation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:25 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004081
19/37

Chronic injuries with symptomatic swan neck deformity
Inability to comply with the splinting regimen
Techniques/procedures
Mallet finger fixation techniques include pinning the DIP joint in extension with or without
tendon repair.

Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Chronic injuries requiring staged reconstruction may be managed nonsurgically if the patient
prefers.
Nondisplaced bony injuries with an intact flexor mechanism
Delay because of competition demands.
Techniques/procedures
A nondisplaced bony injury with an intact flexor mechanism may be protected with the use
of a splint on the DIP joint in extension for 4 to 6 weeks.
Outcomes
Successful outcomes are expected in patients with a minimally displaced bony avulsion
injury.
Because of extensive rehabilitation and likely prolonged inability to participate in sports
activity, some competitive or professional athletes may wish to undergo nonsurgical
treatment or delay surgical treatment until the end of the season. The outcomes of delayed
management may be suboptimal; therefore, delayed management should be considered
only in exceptional situations.35
Halát et al58 reported on 16 patients with a minimally displaced bony FDP avulsion managed
via static DIP joint splinting for 4 weeks, with passive PIP and MCP joint motion beginning at 2
weeks. Excellent outcomes were achieved, with a mean of 70° of DIP joint flexion, 95% tip
pinch strength, and 97% restoration of total active motion; however, a 19% incidence of DIP
joint arthrosis was reported.

Good outcomes are seen with bony avulsions, but results may be less favorable in patients

A purely tendinous avulsion with tendon retraction to the palm requires more urgent surgical
management than a fracture with a minimally displaced bony fragment. Primary tendon
repair in an acute setting can be accomplished via various techniques, such as suture
anchors, all-inside transosseous sutures, or a suture button. Standard techniques are used
for fracture repair or may be combined with suture anchors for small fragments60 (Video 4).
If rigid fixation is attained, early active range of motion is initiated, with a DIP joint splint or,
in more tenuous cases, a forearm-based dorsal blocking splint for protection. Strengthening
can begin at 4 to 6 weeks after bony healing is observed, with return to sports activity at 8 to
12 weeks.

reports recommending passive flexion and active extension only for the initial 3 to 6 weeks.

Outcomes
Excellent functional outcomes and a high rate of return to sport are reported.
Functional therapy exercises include finger motion exercises; tendon gliding exercises; and
the use of elastic bands, putty, and compression balls. Pulley protection via taping or
splinting is used, with duration dependent on the degree of injury. A custom-made
thermoplastic ring splint can used around the proximal (A2) or middle (A4) phalanx to protect
the pulley.68 Various taping patterns have been suggested; the H-tape method described by
Schöffl et al69 has been demonstrated to decrease tendon-to-bone distance and increase
grip strength after pulley rupture.
Gradual return to sports activity can begin at 4 to 6 weeks, with full sport activities resuming
at 6 to 12 weeks, depending on the grade of injury. Taping during sports activity is continued
for 3 to 6 months.40
In a series of 21 climbers with 27 injured fingers, all had excellent outcomes and returned to
climbing within 1 year, with no considerable difference in finger strength.70 In a study of
climbers with a complete pulley rupture managed via custom splinting, 88% returned to
climbing at their preinjury level at a mean of 8.8 months. Ultrasonographic examination
demonstrated improved tendon to bone distance in most patients. Reduced finger range of
motion was reported in 16%, and a measurable decrease in strength was reported in 18%;
however, all the patients expressed satisfaction with their treatment.68 Successful
nonsurgical treatment with full return to sports activity also has been documented in football
and baseball players.40,41

Hook of Hamate Fractures
Overview
Injury often resulting from sporting activities that require gripping action, such as golf,
baseball, tennis, hockey, and other racquet sports
Two types of fractures involve the hamate—a fracture of the body of the hamate and the hook
of the hamate
Although, in general, hook of hamate fractures are rare injuries, they may be more common in
the athletic population. Hook of hamate fractures usually are caused by a direct blow to the
palm or after a fall onto an outstretched hand. These fractures often involve the nondominant
hand because this hand usually is at higher risk.
Associated Injuries
Ulnar nerve and/or median nerve injury; typically presents as paresthesias.
Hamate body fracture
Fourth and fifth carpometacarpal joint dislocation
Tendinopathy or injury to FDP of the little and ring fingers
Patient History
Pain on the volar ulnar aspect of the palm that is worsened by gripping motions
Athletes also may report difficulty with grip secondary to pain or weakness.

Hypothenar Hammer Syndrome
Overview
Injury or thrombosis of the ulnar artery at the wrist from repetitive blunt trauma
Hypothenar hammer syndrome refers to an injury to the ulnar artery at the level of the Guyon
canal caused by repetitive blunt trauma to the hypothenar region. The ulnar artery is relatively
immobile and can be compressed against the hook of the hamate. Repetitive blunt trauma
disrupts the intima of the ulnar artery, which may lead to aneurysm formation and
thrombosis. Clinical findings may include thrombosis and vascular insufficiency in the hand.
Epidemiology
Hypothenar hammer syndrome is a rare condition but is more likely to be observed in manual
laborers, with an incidence as high as 14%.82
Athletes who participate in sports that involve repetitive blunt trauma to the palm of the hand
also are at risk.
Multiple sports, including badminton, baseball, basketball, breakdancing, cycling, mountain
biking, football, golf, hockey, martial arts, snowboarding, soccer, squash, tennis, and
weightlifting, have been associated with the condition.82,83
More common in males, involving the dominant hand84
Other risk factors include smoking, poor protective equipment, and higher training intensity.83

Techniques/procedures
Activity and lifestyle modifications, protective equipment, and vasodilators
Outcomes
Limited evidence exists; however, successful outcomes can be expected in mild cases.
Nonsurgical management is indicated for patients with mild cases, such as those with
Raynaud phenomenon or other mild symptoms.
Smoking cessation and cold avoidance are recommended for all patients. Activity
modifications, if possible, and avoidance of repetitive impact to the area may be helpful. In
addition, the use of protective equipment, such as a padded catcher’s mitt and padded
gloves may be useful. Medications, such as vasodilators (calcium channel blockers),
antiplatelet agents, botulinum toxin, and anticoagulant agents as well as intra-arterial
thrombolytic therapy can be used.83
A small series of 13 athletes, including 9 professional baseball catchers, were successfully
treated nonsurgically via cold avoidance and increased glove padding; two patients required
intra-arterial vasodilator infusion and intravenous anticoagulation. All the baseball catchers
in this series were able to return to professional play without surgical treatment.85
Surgical Management
Indications
Limb-threatening ischemia, aneurysm formation, failed nonsurgical management
Contraindications
Relative contraindications to vascular reconstruction may include persistent smoking,
underlying systemic disease.
Techniques/procedures
Ulnar artery ligation
Arterial reconstruction
Ligation of the vessel may be performed if collateral blood flow through the radial artery is
adequate. This may prevent distal embolization and decrease compression on the ulnar
nerve.
Resection and reconstruction of the diseased arterial segment may be the preferred
treatment option. This may be accomplished via direct end-to-end repair or more commonly
with the use of arterial or venous grafts.
